s0.title: Give OpsWatch its own AWS identity
s0.purpose: OpsWatch needs an identity whose only right is to assume the read-only roles you will create in the next steps.

tabs.server: OpsWatch runs on my computer or a server (Docker)
tabs.aws: OpsWatch runs on AWS (ECS or EC2)

server.i1: Sign in to the AWS console of the account where you want to keep OpsWatch's identity. It can be the account you will monitor.
server.i2: Open IAM → Users → "Create user". Name it opswatch. Leave "Provide user access to the AWS Management Console" unchecked, then click "Next".
server.i3: On "<ui>Set permissions</ui>", keep "<ui>Add user to group</ui>" or choose "<ui>Attach policies directly</ui>" without selecting any policy. Click "<ui>Next</ui>", then "<ui>Create user</ui>".
server.i4: Open the new user → "Permissions" tab → "Add permissions" → "Create inline policy" → "JSON" tab. Replace the content with the policy below, click "Next", name it OpsWatchAssumeRole, then click "Create policy".
server.i5: Open the "<ui>Security credentials</ui>" tab → "<ui>Create access key</ui>" → use case "<ui>Application running outside AWS</ui>" → "<ui>Next</ui>" → "<ui>Create access key</ui>". Copy the "<ui>Access key</ui>" and the "<ui>Secret access key</ui>": the secret is shown only once.
server.i6: In OpsWatch's .env file, set AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY to these two values, and AWS_REGION to your usual region, for example eu-west-1. Check that OPSWATCH_SECRET holds at least 32 random characters (generate them with openssl rand -base64 48): without it, OpsWatch refuses to start. Then restart OpsWatch with docker compose up -d.
server.profileTitle: Docker: keys in .env, profiles for npm run dev
server.profile: With Docker, put AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in .env. An AWS CLI profile (aws configure --profile opswatch, then AWS_PROFILE=opswatch) is meant for npm run dev: the container runs as user 1001 and usually cannot read a mounted ~/.aws/credentials file, whose mode is 600, and SSO profiles also need a writable cache. If the two key variables and AWS_PROFILE are all set, OpsWatch uses the keys and logs a warning at startup.
server.i7: Check: once you have created the connection in step 1, its page no longer warns that OpsWatch has no AWS identity. The "{identityTitle}" card shows the ARN of the opswatch user.

aws.i1: ECS: open the task definition and note the "<ui>Task role</ui>" (not the "<ui>Task execution role</ui>"). EC2: open the instance → "<ui>Security</ui>" tab → note the "<ui>IAM Role</ui>". If there is none, create a role for the ECS task or the EC2 service and attach it.
aws.i2: Open IAM → Roles → that role → "Add permissions" → "Create inline policy" → "JSON". Paste the policy below, click "Next", name it OpsWatchAssumeRole, then click "Create policy".
aws.i3: Redeploy the ECS service ("Update service" → "Force new deployment") or restart OpsWatch on the instance so it picks up the role. There are no keys to configure: leave AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY and AWS_PROFILE empty.

sso.title: What about IAM Identity Center (SSO)?
sso.body: Use IAM, not IAM Identity Center. Identity Center is made for people who sign in: its credentials are temporary and expire after a few hours, so OpsWatch would stop working until someone runs aws sso login again. For a tool that runs all the time, use an IAM user or an ECS or EC2 role. For a quick local try, an SSO profile set through AWS_PROFILE works until the session expires.

ownKey.title: Why not use my own access key?
ownKey.body: It works, but it is not recommended. Your key usually has administrator rights: if OpsWatch's .env, server or database leaks, the whole account is exposed. The dedicated identity can only assume {rolePattern} roles, which are read-only. You can revoke it without touching your own access, and CloudTrail shows clearly what OpsWatch did. Never create access keys for the root user.

s1.title: Create the connection in OpsWatch
s1.purpose: The connection records the account to monitor and generates the unique values its CloudFormation template needs.
s1.i3: Fill in "<ui>{name}</ui>", "<ui>{accountId}</ui>" (the 12 digits of the account to monitor, shown in the account menu at the top right of the AWS console) and "<ui>{regions}</ui>" (the regions where your resources run).
s1.i4: Click "<ui>{submit}</ui>". OpsWatch creates a unique ExternalId and prepares the template for this connection.

s2.title: Deploy the CloudFormation stack in the account to monitor
s2.purpose: The stack creates the read-only role that OpsWatch will assume. Choose one of the three ways below.
s2.region: Create the stack in one region only. IAM is global, so any region works.

console.title: With the AWS console
console.i1: On the OpsWatch connection page, click "<ui>{download}</ui>".
console.i2: In the AWS console of the account to monitor, open <ui>CloudFormation</ui> → <ui>Stacks</ui> → "<ui>Create stack</ui>" → "<ui>With new resources (standard)</ui>".
console.i3: Choose "<ui>Upload a template file</ui>" → "<ui>Choose file</ui>", select the downloaded file, then click "<ui>Next</ui>".
console.i4: In "Stack name", enter {stackName}: the name of the downloaded file without .yaml, also shown in the AWS CLI command of the connection page. Click "Next", then "Next" again.
console.i5: On "<ui>Review and create</ui>", tick "<ui>I acknowledge that AWS CloudFormation might create IAM resources with custom names.</ui>", then click "<ui>Submit</ui>".
console.i6: Wait for the status CREATE_COMPLETE, which takes about one minute.

cli.title: With the AWS CLI
cli.i1: On the connection page, click "<ui>{download}</ui>" and copy the AWS CLI command shown below the button.
cli.i2: Run it from the folder containing the downloaded template, with credentials of the account to monitor. It already contains --capabilities CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM, the command-line equivalent of the acknowledgement box.

launch.title: With Launch Stack (experimental)
launch.note: Experimental: this option has not yet been validated against a real AWS account. Only available when OPSWATCH_TEMPLATE_BUCKET is configured. OpsWatch uploads the template to that bucket, so its identity needs s3:PutObject on it, and the console user of the monitored account must be able to read the template object: allow it with a bucket policy granting s3:GetObject on opswatch/templates/*. When in doubt, download the template instead.
launch.i1: On the connection page, click "<ui>{launchStack}</ui>". The AWS console opens with the template and the stack name already filled in.
launch.i2: Tick the acknowledgement box, then click "<ui>Create stack</ui>".

s3.title: Paste the role ARN
s3.purpose: The ARN tells OpsWatch which role to assume in the monitored account.
s3.i1: In CloudFormation, open the stack → "Outputs" tab → copy the value of RoleArn. It looks like {example}.
s3.i2: On the connection page, paste it into "<ui>{roleArnLabel}</ui>" and click "<ui>{save}</ui>".

s4.title: Run the test
s4.purpose: OpsWatch assumes the role and checks, service by service, what it can read.
s4.i1: On the connection page, click "<ui>{run}</ui>". The result appears after a few seconds.
s4.i2: Read the colour of each line:
s4.green: <ui>Green, "{status}"</ui>: OpsWatch can read this service. Nothing to do.
s4.orange: <ui>Orange, "{status}"</ui>: an action is missing and the line says what you lose. Open "<services>{servicesTitle}</services>" to see why OpsWatch needs it, then add it by updating the stack with a newly downloaded template.
s4.red: <ui>Red</ui>: the connection or the check failed, and the message gives the reason. See "<troubleshooting>{troubleshootingTitle}</troubleshooting>".

ambient.title: Running on AWS
ambient.intro: OpsWatch runs on ECS or EC2 in the account it monitors and reads it with its own task or instance role: no stack and no keys.

s1.title: Find the role OpsWatch runs with
s1.purpose: This role will receive the read-only permissions.

s2.title: Attach the read-only policy
s2.i1: Open <ui>IAM</ui> → <ui>Roles</ui> → that role → "<ui>Add permissions</ui>" → "<ui>Create inline policy</ui>" → "<ui>JSON</ui>".

s3.title: Restart OpsWatch
s3.purpose: A restart makes sure OpsWatch runs with the role and its new permissions.
s3.i1: ECS: open the service → "Update service" → "Force new deployment". EC2: restart OpsWatch on the instance, for example with docker compose restart.

s4.title: Create the connection and run the test
s4.purpose: OpsWatch checks that its role can read the account.
s4.i2: Choose "<ui>{method}</ui>". In "<ui>{accountId}</ui>", enter the ID of the account OpsWatch runs in: this method cannot read another account.
s4.i3: Select the regions and click "<ui>{submit}</ui>", then click "<ui>{run}</ui>" on the connection page.

keys.title: With access keys
keys.intro: For a quick local test. The keys belong to a dedicated read-only user, never to your own IAM user or to the root user.

s1.title: Create a dedicated IAM user
s1.purpose: This user can only read, so a leaked key cannot change anything in your account.
s1.i1: In the AWS console of the account to monitor, open <ui>IAM</ui> → <ui>Users</ui> → "<ui>Create user</ui>".
s1.i2: Name it opswatch-readonly and leave "Provide user access to the AWS Management Console" unchecked. Click "Next", "Next" again, then "Create user".

s2.title: Attach the read-only policy
s2.i1: Open the new user → "<ui>Permissions</ui>" tab → "<ui>Add permissions</ui>" → "<ui>Create inline policy</ui>" → "<ui>JSON</ui>" tab.

s3.title: Create an access key
s3.purpose: OpsWatch signs its AWS requests with this key pair.
s3.i1: Open the "<ui>Security credentials</ui>" tab → "<ui>Create access key</ui>" → use case "<ui>Application running outside AWS</ui>" → "<ui>Next</ui>" → "<ui>Create access key</ui>".
s3.i2: Copy the "<ui>Access key</ui>" and the "<ui>Secret access key</ui>". The secret is shown only once.

s4.title: Save the keys in OpsWatch
s4.purpose: OpsWatch encrypts the keys before storing them.
s4.i2: Choose "<ui>{method}</ui>", fill in the name, the account ID and the regions, then click "<ui>{submit}</ui>".
s4.i3: On the connection page, paste the values into "<ui>{accessKeyId}</ui>" and "<ui>{secretAccessKey}</ui>", then click "<ui>{save}</ui>".
s4.i4: The keys are encrypted and never shown again: only a hint like AKIA…MPLE remains.

s5.title: Run the test and look after the key
s5.purpose: A long-lived key needs care for as long as it exists.
s5.i2: Rotate the key regularly: create a new one, save it in OpsWatch, then delete the old one in IAM.
s5.i3: Delete the key in IAM when you stop using OpsWatch, and switch to the <role>IAM role method</role> whenever you can.

GettingStarted.servicesIntro: The role is deliberately narrower than the AWS ReadOnlyAccess policy, which can read the content of S3 buckets. OpsWatch never reads S3, Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store.

pages.title: What OpsWatch shows
pages.intro: Once a connection passes its permission test, pick it in the top bar, then a region, to open these pages.

items.overview: Overview: health summary and automatic insights (tasks below desired over 10 minutes; high CPU or memory, failed deployments, database CPU and memory, Aurora replica lag, load balancer 5xx errors and unhealthy hosts, alarms firing, over 15 minutes).
items.containers: Containers: ECS services with tasks, CPU and memory, then per service its charts, tasks, events, target groups and log groups.
items.databases: Databases: RDS and Aurora instances with their role, metrics and, when Performance Insights is on, the top SQL statements.
items.loadBalancers: Load balancers: requests, 5xx errors, p95 response time and target health of each application load balancer.
items.alarms: Alarms: CloudWatch alarms by state, with target-tracking autoscaling alarms hidden by default.
items.logs: Logs: pick log groups and run CloudWatch Logs Insights queries over up to 24 hours, with example queries for errors, 5xx responses and slow requests.

pages.refresh: Charts cover 1 hour to 7 days and refresh every 2 minutes while the tab is visible; you can pause the refresh.

billed.logs: {action} is billed by AWS per GB of logs scanned.
billed.cloudwatch: {action} is billed by AWS per metric requested (about USD 0.01 per 1,000 metrics).

ecs.why: List clusters, services and tasks, and read their definitions.
ecs.unlocks: The containers view: services, tasks, deployments and events.

ec2.why: Read instances, network interfaces, security groups and subnets.
ec2.unlocks: Mapping IP addresses and hosts back to services.
ec2.without: IP addresses in logs and database connections stay anonymous.

autoscaling.why: Read the scaling targets and policies of ECS services.
autoscaling.unlocks: Minimum, maximum and target values next to each service.

elb.why: Read load balancers, listeners, rules and target health.
elb.unlocks: Which service receives which traffic, and unhealthy targets.
elb.without: Routing and target health are missing.

rds.why: Read clusters, instances, proxies and events.
rds.unlocks: The databases view, with the real writer and reader roles.

pi.why: Read Performance Insights load, dimensions and SQL text.
pi.unlocks: Top SQL, wait events and the busiest client hosts.
pi.without: You see the CPU but not which query causes it.

cloudwatch.why: Read metric data, list metrics and alarms.
cloudwatch.unlocks: Every chart: CPU, memory, requests, latency and errors.

logs.why: List log groups and run Logs Insights queries.
logs.unlocks: Log search and analyses such as errors per route or the busiest clients.

security.title: Security
security.can1: Read the metadata and metrics of the services listed above.
security.can2: Run the Logs Insights queries you start, which AWS bills.
security.cannot1: Change, create or delete anything in your account.
security.cannot2: Read S3 objects, secrets or parameters.
security.cannot3: Be assumed by any AWS identity other than this OpsWatch instance's: the trust policy names it.
security.externalIdBody: The trust policy already limits the role to this OpsWatch instance's AWS identity, so learning the role ARN is not enough to use it. The ExternalId covers two remaining cases: several OpsWatch instances or tenants sharing one base identity, where one could be pointed at another's role (the confused deputy problem), and a connection configured with the role of another connection. The role only accepts requests that also present the random value generated for its own connection.
security.revokeBody: Delete the CloudFormation stack. The role disappears and OpsWatch loses access immediately. Then remove the connection in OpsWatch.

assumeRole.title: AccessDenied when assuming the role
assumeRole.body: The trust policy does not match: the stack was deployed from an older template, the ExternalId was regenerated, or OpsWatch now runs with another identity. Download the template again and update the stack.

region.title: A region always fails
region.body: The region may be disabled for your account. Enable it in the AWS account settings, or remove it from the connection.

pi.title: Performance Insights is "not applicable"
pi.body: No instance in that region has Performance Insights enabled. Enable it on the database instance to get the top SQL.

scp.title: A permission stays missing although the role has it
scp.body: A service control policy (SCP) of your AWS organization or a permissions boundary may deny the action. Ask your organization administrator.

account.title: The credentials belong to another account
account.body: The role ARN or the keys come from another AWS account than the one entered for the connection. Check the 12-digit account ID.

mockups.consoleAccess: Provide user access to the AWS Management Console - optional
mockups.consoleAccessHint: If you're providing console access to a person, it's a best practice to manage their access in IAM Identity Center.

useCases.compute: Application running on an AWS compute service

mockups.acknowledge: I acknowledge that AWS CloudFormation might create IAM resources with custom names.

hints.CredentialsProviderError: No AWS credentials were found. Set AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in .env, or run OpsWatch on AWS with an ECS task role or an EC2 instance role. Without keys, an AWS_PROFILE set in the shell that starts OpsWatch must name a profile that exists and can be read.
hints.ExpiredToken: The credentials have expired. Replace the temporary keys (with their AWS_SESSION_TOKEN), or run aws sso login again for an SSO profile, then restart OpsWatch.
hints.InvalidClientTokenId: AWS does not recognise this access key ID: it was deleted, deactivated or mistyped. Check AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, then restart OpsWatch.
hints.SignatureDoesNotMatch: The secret access key does not match the access key ID. Check AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY (no extra space or quote), then restart OpsWatch.
hints.Timeout: AWS did not answer within 5 seconds. Check that OpsWatch can reach AWS STS (network, proxy, firewall), then reload this page.
hints.generic: Check OpsWatch's AWS credentials, then reload this page.

picker.title: Log groups

problems.title: Problems
problems.description: What OpsWatch believes is wrong right now, worst first.
problems.empty: Nothing is wrong in this environment.
problems.emptyHint: OpsWatch checks every five minutes. A problem appears here as soon as a detector opens one.
problems.waiting: OpsWatch has not finished its first check of this environment.
problems.waitingHint: The first cycle runs within five minutes of a connection being added.
problems.staleHint: OpsWatch has not been able to evaluate this subject for over an hour, so it is neither confirmed nor cleared.

detail.evidenceDescription: What the detector actually read. Every item is an observed fact.
detail.whyDescription: The score is {score} out of 100. Each term is multiplied by its weight and the total is rescaled over the weight actually available.
detail.unavailableHint: This term is left out rather than counted as zero, and the score is rescaled over the rest.
detail.rescaled: Rescaled over {available} of 100, because not every term could be measured.
detail.floored: Raised to the critical floor: the subject has failed completely.
detail.notFound: That problem does not exist in this environment.

health.title: Health
health.description: Whether this environment is healthy, and what OpsWatch could not check.

statusHint.healthy: Everything OpsWatch checks is within its thresholds.
statusHint.degraded: Something needs attention, or part of this environment could not be read.
statusHint.unknown: OpsWatch has not been able to read this environment, so it cannot say whether production is healthy. This is not the same as everything being fine.

unavailable.denied: OpsWatch is not allowed to read {family} in this account.
unavailable.throttled: AWS is rate-limiting requests for {family}; OpsWatch will try again.

health.noChanges: Nothing has changed in the last day.
health.waiting: OpsWatch has not finished its first check of this environment.
health.waitingHint: The first cycle runs within five minutes of a connection being added.

brief.title: Morning brief
brief.description: What changed since yesterday, and what deserves attention first.
brief.nothingImportant: Nothing is open. There is nothing to start on.
brief.noChanges: Nothing opened or resolved in this period.

summary.unknown: OpsWatch cannot say how production is; it has not been able to read this environment.

brief.opened: {count, plural, =0 {nothing opened} one {# problem opened} other {# problems opened}}
brief.resolved: {count, plural, =0 {nothing resolved} one {# resolved} other {# resolved}}
brief.waiting: OpsWatch has not finished its first check of this environment.
brief.waitingHint: The first cycle runs within five minutes of a connection being added.

errors.title: Errors
errors.description: Errors grouped by what they are, not by how often they happened.
errors.occurrences: {count, plural, one {# time} other {# times}} in the last day
errors.noFrames: This error has no stack trace, so it is grouped by its message and its log group.
errors.noSources: OpsWatch is not reading errors from any log group yet.
errors.noSourcesHint: Error collection is off until you choose a log group. CloudWatch Logs Insights is billed per gigabyte scanned, so OpsWatch never reads one you have not asked it to.
errors.noneEnabled: No log group is switched on for error collection.
errors.noneEnabledHint: Switch one on and OpsWatch will start grouping its errors within fifteen minutes.
errors.empty: No errors have been collected from the log groups you switched on.
errors.emptyHint: OpsWatch reads them every fifteen minutes.
errors.budgetStopped: Error collection stopped for today because it reached its scanning budget.
errors.budgetHint: It resumes tomorrow. Raise OPSWATCH_LOGS_BUDGET_GB_PER_DAY to scan more, knowing that CloudWatch bills per gigabyte.

Settings.title: Settings
Settings.description: Options that apply to every page of this OpsWatch.

refresh.title: Auto-refresh
refresh.label: Refresh interval
refresh.description: How often a page that refreshes itself asks AWS for new data again.
refresh.cost: At this interval a page of about {services} services requests about {metrics} metrics per hour, roughly {usd} per hour: GetMetricData is billed per metric requested.
refresh.costOff: Off costs nothing beyond the metrics of the first page load.

range.title: Time range
range.label: Default time range
range.description: The range a monitoring page opens with. A range in the address bar still wins.

errors.refresh_invalid: Choose one of the offered refresh intervals.
errors.range_invalid: Choose one of the offered time ranges.

status.title: System status
status.description: What OpsWatch knows about itself. This page reads only its own database, so it still works when monitoring does not.
status.collectorNever: The collector has never run. Every page that reports on your environments is reporting on nothing yet.
status.collectorHint: One process collects at a time. It takes a lock and refreshes it every 30 seconds.
status.adminOnly: Only an administrator can see this page.

history.title: Data & history
history.description: Historical collection adds recurring AWS requests, so OpsWatch shows what it would cost before you turn it on.
history.offExplained: While this is off OpsWatch makes no recurring AWS request for history, and every live page keeps working exactly as it does now.
history.estimateCaveat: An estimate from published prices and your discovered resources. It is not a bill, and OpsWatch cannot see your account’s actual rates.
history.lineScanned: Log scanning: about {gigabytes} GB a month
history.volatile: This half moves with how much your application logs, so it is the one that can surprise.

errors.invalid_interval: Choose an interval between 1 and 1440 minutes.
errors.invalid_retention: Choose a retention between 1 and 3650 days.

more.title: More settings
more.historyHint: Whether OpsWatch collects history, what it would cost, and how long it is kept.
more.statusHint: Whether the collector is running, when each job last ran, and the state of the database.
